3 month Muay Thai ED visa in Phuket

Train Muay Thai for 90 days on an education visa, then extend while you keep training. Work hard, Fight easy.

Buy your 3 month course

The visa in short

What the ED visa gives you

The Non-Immigrant ED visa is Thailand's education visa. Learning Muay Thai at a registered gym counts as study, so you can stay and train for months instead of weeks.

  • First stay: 90 days from the day you arrive.
  • Extending: Possible, but via the same pricess.
  • Longest stay: up to 1 year in total from your first entry. After that you leave Thailand and apply again.
  • Visa fee: about 2,000 THB (around 80 USD or EUR) when you apply. It changes slightly by embassy.
  • Work: not allowed on an ED visa, and that includes remote work. If you need to work online, the DTV is the better fit.

You do not have to be a fighter. We coach complete beginners, fitness students and fighters.

Benefits

Why train here for 3 months

Time is what makes the difference. Here is what you get.

01

Real progress

Weeks of steady training with technical coaching. Your basics get sharp and your fitness builds.

02

A set routine

Group classes Monday to Saturday. You always know where to be and what you are working on.

03

Recovery on site

Herbal steam room, dry sauna, ice bath and yoga. Your body keeps up with your training.

04

Stay and eat here

Pangea Resort lakeside bungalows are on site. Pangea Cafe serves healthy, seed oil free food.

Documents

What you need to apply

  • Passport valid for at least 6 more months
  • A recent passport photo
  • Proof of money for your stay, usually a bank statement (around 20,000 THB is often asked)
  • Your enrolment letter from the gym
  • The letter from the education or sports authority that goes with it

Apply online at thaievisa.go.th if your country is on it, or at a Thai embassy or consulate. Processing usually takes 1 to 3 weeks, so start at least a month before you fly. We tell you exactly which documents to send and help with the gym side.

How it works

How to get your ED visa

  1. Buy your courseChoose 3 months or more of training on our prices page and pay online. Want to live on site? Add a bungalow at Pangea Resort.
  2. Send us your detailsMessage us on WhatsApp with your arrival date and passport name. We start your visa documents straight away.
  3. Get your documents and applyWe prepare the gym paperwork. You apply online at thaievisa.go.th or at a Thai embassy with it.
  4. Arrive and trainGroup classes Monday to Saturday. Train regularly: immigration can ask for your attendance when you extend.
  5. Extend in PhuketBefore your 90 days end, extend at Phuket Immigration with your school letter, attendance record and 1,900 THB in cash.
Prices

What 3 months costs

  • Training Only, 3 months: 18,000 THB. Unlimited group Muay Thai.
  • Training + Recovery, 3 months: 28,000 THB. Adds the sauna, steam room and ice bath.
  • Fitness Zone add on: 7,000 THB for 3 months.
  • ED visa paperwork: message us for the current fee.

Government fees are paid by you to the embassy and immigration: about 2,000 THB for the visa and 1,900 THB for each extension.

See all prices
Compare

ED visa or DTV?

ED visa suits you if you want to train for 3 months to a year and not work while you are here. The visa fee is low and you extend every 90 days.

DTV suits you if you want longer, or you work online. It is a 5 year visa with stays of up to 180 days per entry, and it allows remote work. You need to be 20 or older and show about 500,000 THB in savings, and the visa fee is higher.

Not sure? Read our DTV page or message us and we will tell you which one fits.

Questions about the ED visa

Do I need Muay Thai experience?

No. We coach beginners, people who want fitness, and fighters.

How long can I stay?

90 days on arrival. You can extend inside Thailand while you keep training, up to 1 year in total from your first entry.

Can I extend in Phuket?

Yes, at Phuket Immigration. Bring your passport, a photo, your school letter, your attendance record, proof of where you stay and 1,900 THB in cash.

Can I work on an ED visa?

No. Work of any kind is not allowed, including remote work for clients abroad. Look at the DTV if you need to work.

Do I need to report my address?

If you stay more than 90 days in a row, you report your address to immigration every 90 days. It can usually be done online.

Can I stay at the gym?

Yes. Pangea Resort lakeside bungalows are on site. See book your stay.

Are the visa rules fixed?

No. Thai immigration rules and fees can change. This page was checked in October 2026. Message us before you book flights and we will give you the current picture.

Ready for 3 months of real training?

Buy your course today, add a stay if you want one, and we will start your visa documents.

Muay Thai for beginners in Phuket

Never trained before? Perfect. Our coaches start you with the basics and build from there, at your pace.

Your first class

What happens on day one

Come ten minutes early and check in at the desk. Wear shorts and a t shirt. Bring gloves if you have them, or ask at the desk.

You will warm up, learn the stance and guard, then the basic punches and kicks. A coach will hold pads for you and correct the small things that make the biggest difference.

Why start here

Built for people learning properly

01

Coaches who can teach

Every trainer has fought, and every one has been taught how to coach beginners.

02

A clear structure

Each class follows a plan, so you are not left guessing what to do next.

03

No ego

Respect, humility and good humour. Nobody cares how fit you are on day one.

04

Recovery on site

Ice bath, sauna and yoga help you train again tomorrow.

Your first weeks

How beginners usually progress

  1. Week 1Stance, guard, jab, cross and the round kick. Short rounds while your body adjusts.
  2. Week 2Combinations, defence and the teep. You start to feel the rhythm on the pads.
  3. Weeks 3 and 4Knees, elbows and light technical sparring if you want it. No pressure to fight, ever.

Beginner questions

Am I too unfit to start?

No. Classes are for everyone. Go at your own pace, take breaks when you need to, and you will be fitter within a couple of weeks.

Do I have to spar or fight?

No. Sparring is always optional, and many of our guests never fight. Read no, you do not have to fight.

What should I buy first?

A single class or a week pass is the best way to start. See prices.

Am I too old?

Probably not. Read am I too old to learn Muay Thai.

How Much Does It Cost to Train Muay Thai in Phuket? 2026 Guide

Phuket is blessed with a lot of Muay Thai gyms. It probably has more per person than almost anywhere else in Thailand. That is great for choice, but it makes the question "how much does it cost?" hard to answer, because no two gyms offer the same thing.

Some gyms train fighters only. Some train everyone. Some offer accommodation, some do not. And the accommodation itself varies massively. Many smaller gyms that say they have accommodation are really renting out a basic room somewhere nearby.

So the honest answer is: it depends on what you want. Here is how to work it out.

The short answer

  • Basic fighter setup: if you are a fighter and you do not mind a single bed and a shared bathroom, there are plenty of options. Expect to pay around 20,000 to 30,000 THB a month for training and a room.
  • Well known gym, comfortable stay: at one of the better known gyms, such as Phuket King or AKA Thailand, you will spend a little more.
  • Your own room with comfort and extras: a private room with its own bathroom and air conditioning, in a nice environment, plus meals, privates and extras, usually comes to around 30,000 to 80,000 THB a month.

What changes the price

Before you compare gyms, be clear about what you are actually looking for.

Your room
- Do you mind basic, or do you want comfort?
- Do you want air conditioning?
- Do you want your own bathroom?
- Do you want meals included?

The gym
- Do you want a classic, old school Thai gym?
- Or something cleaner and more modern?

The extras
- Yoga?
- Grappling?
- A weights gym?
- A spa, sauna or ice bath?

Every one of these affects the final price.

Time of year

Season is another big variable. Phuket's high season runs from November to early April, with December and January the peak months. Prices are usually at their highest then.

After that comes what we call the green season, or rainy season. Prices are often cheaper, gyms are quieter, and it can be a great time to train. If you are on a budget, it is a great time to come.

Build your package and get an instant quote

What to Pack for a Muay Thai Camp in Phuket

Packing for a Muay Thai trip is easier than most people think. Phuket is hot all year, you will sweat through everything, and you can buy most things here. Here is what is worth bringing, and what is not.

Training gear

  • Gloves: if you have a pair you like, bring them. If not, you can buy good Thai gloves here.
  • Hand wraps: bring two or three pairs. They need to dry between sessions.
  • Shin guards: only if you plan to spar.
  • Mouthguard: essential if you spar. Bring your own.
  • Shorts: two or three pairs of training shorts. Thai shorts are cheap and easy to find.
  • Tops: light, quick dry t shirts or vests. You will change after every session.

Clothes for the heat

  • Light, breathable clothes for the day.
  • Flip flops or sandals. You take your shoes off before stepping into the gym in Thailand.
  • Something to cover your shoulders and knees if you plan to visit temples.
  • A light rain jacket in the rainy season.

Recovery and health basics

  • A refillable water bottle. You will drink a lot.
  • Electrolytes. Easy to find here, but useful to have from day one.
  • Plasters and tape for blisters on your feet.
  • Sun cream and insect repellent.
  • Any medication you normally take, with the packaging.

At Phuket King you will also have an ice bath, herbal steam room and dry sauna on site, so you do not need to bring any recovery gear.

Documents and money

  • Your passport, with at least six months left on it.
  • Travel insurance that covers sport. Check the small print for combat sports.
  • A bank card that works abroad. Many places also take card and PromptPay QR payments.
  • If you plan a long stay, read our guide to the DTV visa.

What not to bring

  • Too many clothes. Laundry is cheap and quick in Phuket.
  • Heavy jeans and jackets. You will not wear them.
  • Brand new gloves you have never tested. Break them in first, or buy here.

Before you fly

Book your first week of training or your room, and message us with your arrival day. If you stay at Pangea Resort, your bungalow is one minute from the ring and group Muay Thai is included when you book with us. See free rooms.

Questions about what to bring? Message us on WhatsApp.

posts.description: Never trained and a little nervous? Muay Thai is one of the most welcoming sports you can start. Here is what it is really like, and how to choose a gym that is safe for beginners.
posts.html:
19 October 2026

Is Muay Thai Safe for Beginners? An Honest Answer

We get asked this a lot, usually a little nervously: "I have never done Muay Thai before. Is that okay?"

Yes. Absolutely.

Muay Thai has fighting in its nature, but for a beginner it is one of the most relaxed sports you can start, and it is kind to your body. A good gym, with a good philosophy, will be genuinely happy to have you and will love helping you begin your Muay Thai journey.

Fighters are some of the gentlest people you will meet

It surprises a lot of people, but some of the gentlest, kindest people you will ever meet are Thai Muay Thai fighters. They are calm, humble and patient, and most of them love teaching beginners.

What really decides how a gym feels is its culture. The trainers and the members make the atmosphere. So choose a gym that:

  • is happy to have beginners and welcomes them,
  • has a proper programme for beginners,
  • has a good history of teaching people from day one.

So, is it dangerous?

No. That could not be further from the truth for someone starting out.

Like any sport, you need to listen to your body and manage your expectations. But a beginner class is pad work, bag work, technique and fitness. Nobody throws you into a fight.

If anything, Muay Thai is the opposite of dangerous. It builds confidence and self esteem, and people who train tend to be calmer and less likely to be aggressive outside the gym, not more.

What a beginner class really involves

  • A warm up and stretching.
  • Learning the stance, guard and footwork.
  • The basic strikes: jab, cross, round kick and teep.
  • Rounds on the pads with a coach.
  • Bag work and conditioning.

What about sparring?

Sparring is optional. Many people train for years and never spar hard or fight. Read no, you do not have to fight.

If you do want to spar:

  • Choose a gym with a good sparring culture, one that does not like aggressive sparring.
  • Make sure you are matched fairly with someone at your level who controls their power.
  • If someone hits you hard, by accident or on purpose, just walk away. Tell a coach, and do not spar with that person again.

How to start safely

  • Start slowly. One class a day for the first week is plenty.
  • Learn technique first. Good technique protects your joints. That is why we teach technique first at Phuket King.
  • Drink water and electrolytes. Phuket is hot and you will sweat a lot.
  • Rest and recover. Sleep, eat well, and use the ice bath, herbal steam room and sauna.
  • Tell your coach. If something hurts, say so, and they will adapt the session.
  • Train within your level. There is no rush.

The bottom line

Train at a welcoming gym, stay within your level and listen to your body, and Muay Thai is a safe, friendly sport to start, at any age and any fitness level.

Our beginners page explains your first class and your first weeks. No booking needed for group classes. Just turn up ten minutes early, or message us on WhatsApp with any question.

Where to Stay in Phuket for Muay Thai Training

Where you stay in Phuket makes a bigger difference to your training than most people expect. Training twice a day means four trips a day if you stay far from the gym. Here is how to choose.

The golden rule: stay close to the gym

The best place to stay is wherever you can walk to training. When the gym is five minutes away, you train more, rest more and spend less on taxis. When it is thirty minutes away, you start skipping the afternoon class.

Patong

Patong is Phuket's busiest beach town, with nightlife, restaurants and shopping. It is great for a holiday, but it is loud late at night, and early nights matter when you train in the morning.

Chalong

Chalong in the south of the island is home to several gyms and is popular with long stay fighters. It is quieter than Patong but further from the west coast beaches.

Kathu

Kathu sits between Patong and Phuket Town, in the green middle of the island. It is quieter, greener and more local, but still a short drive from the beaches. This is where Phuket King is.

Staying at the gym

The easiest option of all is to stay where you train. At Phuket King, Pangea Resort has eleven air conditioned lakeside bungalows one minute from the ring. Your day looks like this:

  • Walk to the morning class.
  • Breakfast at Pangea Cafe, a few steps away.
  • Ice bath, sauna or a nap by the lake.
  • Afternoon or evening class.

When you book your room directly with us, group Muay Thai is included for one person for your whole stay. See free rooms and prices.

What to look for, wherever you stay

  • Distance to the gym: walking distance is best.
  • Air conditioning: good sleep is good recovery.
  • Healthy food nearby: you will be hungry.
  • Quiet nights: you will want to sleep early.

Long stays

If you want to train for months, the DTV visa lets you stay up to 180 days per visit, and we handle the training paperwork for you.

How to Apply for the DTV Visa Through Muay Thai: The Real Process, Step by Step (2026)

A lot of DTV guides online are written by people who have never trained in Thailand or sent a student through the process. This one is different. We've been issuing DTV Soft Power documents since the visa launched, and Phuket King was one of the first accredited gyms in Phuket to do it.

This is what applying actually looks like, from buying your course with us to getting through the door at the gym. No fluff, and nothing sugar coated.

Rules are correct as of September 2026. Embassies change their requirements often, so always check your own embassy's website before you apply.

First: What Changed on 31 August 2026

Two big changes came in on 31 August 2026, and they affect everyone applying from now on.

  • You must apply in your country of residence. You now apply through the Thai embassy or consulate for your country of nationality, or the country where you are a permanent resident. No more flying to Vientiane or Penang to apply there. A tourist stamp, hotel booking or temporary work permit does not count as residence.
  • You now need a police check. You need a police clearance certificate from your country of nationality or the country you apply from. It must be in English or Thai, or come with a certified translation. Some embassies accept one up to 6 months old, while others want it within 3 months.

We made a video breaking down both changes. Watch it here.

Step 1: Choose Your Course

You can't get a DTV without a real training commitment, and embassies are paying closer attention to what you buy. Short, cheap courses are more likely to be questioned. Longer commitments generally carry more weight.

We don't sell paperwork. We sell training. Every DTV document we issue is backed by a real course that you're expected to attend.

For people who want flexibility, we've launched the DTV Group Class Pass:

  • 60 group Muay Thai classes
  • 12 months to use them
  • Come and go as you like. Travel for a month or two, then come back and pick up where you left off
  • Your 12 months start from your first class, and that class must be within 3 months of purchase
  • Group classes only. Open gym and fitness zone access are not included

See full details of the DTV Group Class Pass

Step 2: Pay and Receive Your DTV Documents

Once your course is paid in full, we send you everything the embassy needs from the gym side. This includes:

  • Your acceptance letter with your course details and dates
  • Your payment receipt
  • The gym's official registration and accreditation documents

Tip: Tell us your planned arrival date before we issue your letter. The dates on your letter should match your application.

Step 3: Get Your Bank Statement Right

This is where most people get caught out.

  • You need at least 500,000 baht (or the equivalent in your currency) in your account.
  • Most embassies want to see around 3 months of statements, with the balance held the whole time. Some ask for less, some for more. Check yours.
  • It needs to be an official statement, stamped by the bank or digitally certified. Screenshots from your banking app won't cut it.
  • It should be a normal savings or current account. Don't rely on crypto, investment accounts or credit limits.

The big mistake: moving a lump sum into your account the week before you apply. Embassies want to see money that's been sitting there. A sudden deposit looks like borrowed money and is one of the most common reasons for rejection. If you need to move funds, do it months ahead.

Step 4: Get Your Police Check Early

Start this as soon as you've decided to apply. Police checks can take anywhere from a few days to several weeks, depending on your country. For example, a UK police certificate usually takes 10 to 20 working days as standard.

Don't get it too early either. If your embassy wants it within 3 months and yours is 4 months old, it will be rejected.

Step 5: Gather Everything Else

Along with your course documents, bank statement and police check, you'll usually need:

  • A passport valid for at least 6 months, with blank pages
  • A recent passport photo on a white or light background
  • Proof of residence in the country you're applying from
  • Your accommodation plans in Thailand
  • Proof of travel plans or a flight booking

Scan everything clearly. Blurry or cropped documents slow things down and can lead to extra requests.

Step 6: Submit Your Application

Most applications go through the official Thai e-Visa website (thaievisa.go.th), under the embassy for your country. The fee is around 10,000 baht, paid in your local currency, and it isn't refundable.

Processing usually takes between a few working days and a few weeks, depending on the embassy and how busy it is. Apply at least 4 to 6 weeks before you want to travel, and don't book anything you can't change until your visa is approved.

Step 7: After You Apply

Sometimes the embassy comes back with questions or asks for more documents. This is normal and doesn't mean you'll be rejected.

This is where we help. We support you and give advice through the whole process, from choosing your course to answering follow-up requests from the embassy.

If you are rejected, it's almost always because of the application itself: the bank statement, a missing document or an outdated police check. That's why getting Steps 3 to 5 right matters so much.

Step 8: Entering Thailand

Your DTV is approved. It's a 5-year visa with stays of up to 180 days per entry. Now you need to get through immigration.

An approved visa lets you ask to enter Thailand. It doesn't guarantee you'll be let in. The immigration officer at the airport makes the final call, and that's why it pays to arrive prepared.

Put together one neat folder with printed copies of:

  • Your DTV approval (the visa approval document from your application)
  • Your acceptance letter and receipts from our gym
  • All your other application documents, including your bank statements and police check

And have the standard entry requirements ready:

  • 20,000 baht in readily available funds. Cash is the simplest way to show it.
  • An onward travel ticket: an open return flight, or a train or bus ticket to another country.
  • Proof of where you're staying once you arrive, like a booking confirmation or rental agreement.

You might not be asked for any of it. Plenty of people walk straight through. But these are real entry requirements, and you don't want to be the one standing at the counter scrolling through your emails. If an officer asks, you hand over the folder and you're through.

Respect the visa. Respect the Kingdom.

Getting a DTV doesn't put you above the law. You're a guest here. Follow Thai law, respect the culture and the people, and use the visa for what it's for. The DTV exists because Thailand chose to open its doors to people who want to live, train and learn here. Every holder who abuses it makes it harder for the next person, and every holder who respects it helps keep that door open.

Step 9: Train

Now the fun part starts. Come to the gym, take your first class and your 12 months begin. Train hard for a few weeks, travel, come back and keep going. What is important when you start Muay Tha?

Re-entering Thailand: Most DTV holders re-enter without being asked about their training, but it's smart to be ready. Keep your acceptance letter and receipt with you, along with photos from training. Where possible, we'll help with anything you need to show at immigration.

Refunds and Your Visa Outcome

Our standard refund policy covers all our packages, including DTV courses. Your visa outcome doesn't affect your purchase or your refund terms. Your course and refund terms stay the same whether your DTV is approved, rejected or delayed. Embassy fees are paid to the embassy and are never refundable.

We tell you this upfront because we'd rather you apply prepared than apply hopeful.

Quick Checklist

  • ☐ Course purchased and DTV documents received
  • ☐ 500,000+ baht held in your account, with official statements for the period your embassy asks for
  • ☐ Police check issued within your embassy's time limit
  • ☐ Passport with 6+ months validity
  • ☐ Passport photo
  • ☐ Proof of residence
  • ☐ Accommodation and travel plans
  • ☐ Application submitted through the correct embassy
  • ☐ For arrival: a printed folder with your DTV approval, gym receipts and all your documents
  • ☐ For arrival: 20,000 baht in readily available funds, an onward ticket and proof of accommodation

DTV Visa FAQs

Can I get a DTV visa for Muay Thai training?

Yes. Muay Thai is one of the approved Soft Power activities for the DTV. You need to enrol in a course with an accredited gym, and the gym issues the documents you need for your application.

How much money do I need for a DTV visa?

You need at least 500,000 baht, or the equivalent, in your bank account. Most embassies want to see around 3 months of official statements showing the money was held the whole time.

Do I need a police check for the DTV visa?

Yes. Since 31 August 2026, you need a police clearance certificate from your country of nationality or the country you apply from. Some embassies accept one up to 6 months old, while others want it within 3 months.

Can I apply for the DTV visa from a neighbouring country?

Not anymore. Since 31 August 2026, you must apply in your country of nationality or permanent residence.

What do I need when entering Thailand on a DTV?

Bring a folder with printed copies of your DTV approval, gym receipts and application documents. You also need 20,000 baht in readily available funds, an onward travel ticket and proof of accommodation.

Do I get a refund if my DTV visa is rejected?

At Phuket King, your visa outcome doesn't affect your purchase or your refund terms. Our standard refund policy covers all our packages.

Ready to Start?

If you want to train in Phuket on your own schedule, the DTV Group Class Pass was built for you. Questions about your situation? Message us and we'll give you a straight answer.

View the DTV Group Class Pass

13 September 2026

Thailand DTV Visa Rules Have Changed: What You Need to Know From 31 August 2026

If you're planning to apply for Thailand's Destination Thailand Visa (DTV), there have been some important changes.

And if you're already in Thailand and were planning to make a quick trip to somewhere like Laos or Vietnam to submit your application, this is particularly important.

From 31 August 2026, new requirements apply to DTV applications.

There is a little more paperwork involved, but we don't necessarily see the changes as a bad thing. In fact, as the DTV matures, we think they could ultimately make the whole process clearer and more straightforward for genuine applicants.

You can't simply apply from any country anymore

This is probably the biggest change.

Previously, it became quite common for people already travelling or staying in Thailand to leave the country and submit their DTV application from a nearby country.

Laos and Vietnam, for example, became popular options.

Under the new requirements, applicants need to submit their application in a country where they are either a citizen or permanent resident, with evidence to support this.

So if you're currently in Thailand, don't assume you can simply book a flight to a neighbouring country, stay for a few days and apply for your DTV while you're there.

Before making any travel arrangements, check where you are actually eligible to apply.

Criminal record checks are now required

There's another important change.

Applicants are now required to provide a criminal record clearance certificate, more commonly referred to as a police check or police clearance.

The exact name and format of this document will depend on your country. There isn't one universal "DTV police check".

Different countries have different authorities and procedures for obtaining criminal record certificates, so you'll need to find out which official document applies to you.

This is also something worth arranging early. Depending on your country and where you currently are, obtaining the correct police check may take some time.

What does this mean if you're already in Thailand?

The main thing is simply to plan ahead.

If you've been considering a DTV and thought you could sort everything out by making a short trip to Laos, Vietnam or another nearby country, don't book that trip based on old information.

Check the latest requirements first, you can use our DTV webpage hereto see many frequently asked questios

Make sure you know where you're eligible to submit your application, what evidence of citizenship or permanent residence is required, and what criminal record documentation you'll need.

A little preparation now could save a lot of wasted time later.

What about a DTV for Muay Thai?

Muay Thai is one of the activities that can form the basis of a DTV application.

At Phuket King Muay Thai, we provide genuine Muay Thai training programmes along with the supporting documentation for customers purchasing an eligible course. Check your options here.

There is an important distinction here though.

We provide Muay Thai training and supporting course documentation. We don't issue visas.

The decision to approve or refuse a DTV application belongs to the relevant Thai authorities, and every applicant is responsible for meeting the current requirements.

That's also why we're publishing updates like this.

We deal with people from all over the world who want to come to Thailand and train Muay Thai, so when something significant changes, we'd rather tell people about it than have somebody discover it after they've booked a flight.

Our thoughts on the new DTV rules

Although these changes mean a little more preparation for applicants, we actually think they could be positive in the long run.

The DTV is still relatively new.

Like any new visa programme, there's going to be a period where the system develops as embassies, applicants and businesses start using it in the real world.

We've already seen some of that.

Different embassies can interpret documentation differently. Applicants aren't always sure what they're supposed to provide. Gyms and other businesses have also had to learn what supporting documents are expected from them.

As the DTV matures, we'd expect that to improve.

Embassies should become clearer about exactly what they expect to see. Gyms should know exactly what documentation they need to provide. The formats should become more standardised.

And most importantly, you, the applicant, should know what you need before you start the process.

That's where we think these changes could ultimately help.

Yes, there may be more paperwork involved at the beginning. But if the result is a clearer and more consistent system, the application itself should become more streamlined for genuine applicants.

Instead of sending documents backwards and forwards, wondering whether something will be accepted, or getting different information depending on where you apply, hopefully everybody involved starts working from the same playbook.

For us, that's a good thing.

We want somebody coming to Thailand to train Muay Thai to know what they need, submit the correct documents the first time and have as straightforward an experience as possible.

The DTV is maturing

We don't see these changes as the end of the DTV or something people should panic about.

We see them as part of a relatively new visa programme beginning to mature.

There will probably continue to be adjustments as the system develops, which is why it's important to check the current requirements rather than relying on information from six months or a year ago.

If you're applying, always check the latest requirements of the Thai embassy or consulate responsible for your particular application before paying for flights or making travel arrangements.

We'll continue to share important DTV updates when they affect people coming to Thailand for Muay Thai.

And if you're interested in training at Phuket King and want to know about our DTV-eligible Muay Thai programmes, you can see our dedicatedDTV webpage here, or get in touch. We can explain the training programme and documentation we provide, so you know exactly what to expect from our side of the process.

Phuket King Muay Thai, not just another gym

‘Work hard, fight easy’

Do you need your own gloves?

How many times a week should you train?

And probably the biggest one, does it actually matter which gym you choose?

So rather than us sitting down and writing another guide telling beginners what they should do, we asked our coaches.

And as you'll see in the video, they don't always agree.

That's probably a good thing.

Do beginners need private Muay Thai classes?

Private training can make a massive difference, especially at the beginning.

You've got a coach watching only you. They can pick up on things you might not even realise you're doing wrong, your stance, balance, guard, how you're turning your hip, where your hands are going.

You can get a lot done in an hour.

But does that mean you have to take private classes before joining a group?

No.

A good group class should still be suitable for somebody walking into a Muay Thai gym for the first time.

We get complete beginners training alongside people who have been doing Muay Thai for years. The job of the coach is to understand who is standing in front of them and coach them accordingly.

Privates can speed things up. They can build confidence. They're great if there's something specific you want to work on.

But you don't need to disappear for ten private sessions before you're "good enough" to join everyone else.

You're a beginner. You're allowed to be a beginner.

Do you need to be fit before starting Muay Thai?

This one comes up all the time.

"I want to try Muay Thai, but I'm going to get fit first."

Why?

Muay Thai will get you fit.

Nobody expects you to arrive on your first day able to smash pads for five rounds without getting tired.

You'll probably get tired. That's normal.

Your fitness builds as you train.

The same goes for flexibility, coordination and balance. Some people pick things up quickly, some don't. It doesn't really matter.

Just start. Check our schedule here for ideas of how many classes run a day

How often should a beginner train?

There's no magic number.

If you're here on holiday and you've only got a week, you might want to train every day.

If you live here and you're fitting Muay Thai around work and normal life, two or three sessions a week might be perfect.

Consistency matters more than going crazy for your first week, destroying yourself, and then not coming back for ten days.

Your body needs a bit of time to adapt as well.

Does equipment matter?

You don't need to turn up on day one looking like a professional fighter.

Basic training gear is enough.

As you start training regularly, then yes, it's worth getting decent gloves and equipment that fits properly and that you actually like using.

But don't let not owning all the gear become another excuse for not starting.

Does choosing the right Muay Thai gym matter?

For us, this is probably the big one.

Especially for a beginner.

Your first experience of Muay Thai can shape how you see the sport.

A beginner doesn't need watered-down Muay Thai. They need proper Muay Thai taught at a level they can understand.

There's a difference.

You want coaches who will correct you, explain things, and actually teach technique rather than just trying to make you exhausted.

You also want somewhere you feel comfortable asking questions and making mistakes.

Because you will make mistakes.

Everyone does.

That's training.

You don't need to arrive fit.

So what is actually important?

You don't need to know how to fight.

You don't need perfect equipment.

You don't even need to know what you're doing.

Find a good gym. Listen to your coaches. Learn the technique properly. Train consistently.

Everything else comes.

And if you're thinking about trying Muay Thai for the first time in Phuket,come and train with us.

Complete beginners are welcome.

Phuket King Muay Thai, not just another gym

‘Work hard, fight easy’

Stop Kicking the heavy bag wrong

Heavy Bag Training for Beginners: Master the Basics Before You Get Hurt

Heavy bag training is an art in itself. Many gyms don't actually teach it correctly, and honestly, many coaches don't either. You learn at a Muay Thai gym, they show you some techniques, you do pad work, and then they tell you to go hit the bags. But we often see people hitting bags with no real clear aim, no technique, and it becomes very ineffective.

This guide shows you how to hit the bag properly. We're going to start with one of the most complex and most iconic Muay Thai strikes: the roundhouse kick. And why? Because if you kick the bag incorrectly, you don't just waste your time and progress slowly. You also risk real injury.

Why Kicking Technique Matters: The Real Risks

Watch this breakdown of the most common kicking error:

[Video: Stop Kicking the heavy bag wrong! - PhuketKing]

The heavy bag is heavy. If you kick it incorrectly, not only will you not progress and your technique will be slow and sloppy, but you stand a real risk of injury. We're not just talking about minor soreness. Improper kicking can lead to:

  • Twisted ankles
  • Swollen feet
  • Overextended ankle joints
  • Damaged standing knee and hips

This happens more often than you'd think. The good news: understanding the concept and learning proper technique prevents all of it.

The Core Principles of Proper Heavy Bag Training

1. Stance and Balance: The Foundation for Everything

Before you strike, you need a solid foundation. Start by getting nice and comfortable with your stance. Let the bag swing back and forth. Watch its rhythm. As the bag comes in, that's when you strike.

Your stance should feel natural, not rigid. Your hands should be up in a defensive position at all times. As you kick, keep your hands up to protect your head. The hand on the same side as your kick should fall slightly as you rotate, helping you generate full rotation through your body.

This comfort with your stance is what allows technique to flow. Don't overcomplicate it, but don't skip it either. This is where everything starts.

2. Technique is King. Speed and Power Come Later.

This is the most important principle. Technique is king. Don't overextend. Don't rush to throw hard.

Most beginners make the mistake of trying to generate power before they've mastered the movement. This is backwards. Here's the correct order:

  1. Perfect your technique slowly
  2. Add speed as you get comfortable
  3. Power will naturally follow as you combine speed with proper form

Power comes from mass and speed together. Right now, ignore power. Focus on getting comfortable with the movement, the rotation, the stance, and the timing of when to strike. As you improve and progress, you'll naturally get faster. The power will come.

The heavy bag doesn't lie to you like a training partner might. If your technique is sloppy, you'll feel it. If you're overextending, you'll pay for it with injury. So respect the process and slow down.

3. The Roundhouse Kick: Rotation and Energy Transfer

The roundhouse kick is one of the most iconic and effective Muay Thai strikes. It's also one of the most dangerous to perform incorrectly on a heavy bag. Here's the proper way.

The Rotation: Your standing foot should rotate about 90 to 180 degrees. Your hips should rotate the same amount. You're not kicking straight up. You're kicking up and around and a little bit forward. The power comes from this rotation, not from your leg.

The Whip Concept: Think of your leg as a whip, not as a baseball bat. There's no power in the leg itself until it actually hits the bag. Your leg is loose, controlled, but not rigid. When your leg makes contact with the bag, that's when you tighten up everything and allow the energy to transfer to the bag.

What Not to Do: Don't overextend. Don't throw hard and fast before you master the technique. Beginners who ignore this get twisted ankles, swollen feet, and overextended joints. Your training partner can adjust for your mistakes. The bag cannot. So respect it by slowing down and perfecting the technique first.

4. Breathing and Pacing

Most beginners hold their breath. This tires you faster and reduces power output.

Proper heavy bag breathing:

  • Exhale sharply with each strike (jab, cross, kick)
  • Inhale when resetting between combinations
  • Maintain a steady rhythm, not gasping

Pacing strategy for beginners:

  • 3 rounds of 3 minutes (with 1-minute rest) is a solid start
  • Go 50% intensity. You're building technique, not trying to KO the bag
  • As you improve, gradually increase intensity and duration

5. Recovery and Smart Training

Heavy bag work is intense. Recovery is where the magic happens.

  • Rest days matter: Don't hit the bag hard more than 3-4 times per week
  • Wrist wraps are essential: They protect your wrists and prevent cumulative injury
  • Hand padding: Use proper hand wraps or gloves (16oz gloves for beginners is standard)
  • Stretch after: Shoulders, hips, and legs take the most impact
  • Listen to pain: Soreness is normal; sharp pain is not

Common Beginner Injuries (And How to Prevent Them)

Wrist Strain

Cause: Improper punch alignment; your wrist isn't supported. Prevention: Wrap your hands correctly. Your wrist should stay neutral throughout the punch.

Shoulder Impingement

Cause: Throwing wild hooks or bringing elbows too high. Prevention: Keep elbows at 45 degrees, not flared out. Build rotator cuff strength with light band work 2-3 times weekly.

Knee Pain

Cause: Kicking with a locked knee or pivoting incorrectly. Prevention: Always bend your supporting leg. Rotate from the hip, not the knee.

Ankle Rolls

Cause: Poor footwork or rushing combinations. Prevention: Focus on controlled movement over speed. Wear proper boxing shoes if possible.

Your First Week: A Sample Routine

Day 1: Basic Punching

  • Warm-up: 2 minutes light jab practice
  • 3 rounds of jab-cross-jab combinations
  • Rest 1 minute between rounds
  • Cool-down: shoulder stretches

Day 2: Rest or Light Cardio

Day 3: Punching + Light Kicks

  • Warm-up: hand and wrist circles
  • Round 1: jab-cross combinations
  • Round 2: add 3 front kicks per side
  • Round 3: mixed combinations
  • Cool-down: full body stretch

Day 4: Rest

Day 5: Mixed Combinations

  • Warm-up: shadowbox (no bag)
  • 3 rounds of jab-cross-hook with occasional kicks
  • Focus on form over power
  • Cool-down: hip flexor and hamstring stretches

Days 6-7: Rest

This gives you two quality training days while prioritizing recovery.

Gear You Actually Need

  • Hand wraps: Non-negotiable. They support your wrists and knuckles.
  • Gloves: 16oz for beginners; heavier gloves reduce hand speed but are easier on joints
  • Heavy bag: 70-100 lbs is standard; start lighter if you're small
  • Wrapping instructions: Watch a tutorial. Bad wraps undo all your protection
  • Boxing shoes (optional): Provide ankle support; regular sneakers work initially

The Mental Game

Heavy bag training isn't just physical. It builds discipline, focus, and stress relief. But beginners often make these mistakes:

  • Ego training: Trying to match experienced fighters' intensity on day one
  • Ignoring form: Sloppy reps build bad habits that are hard to break
  • Skipping fundamentals: The basics never get old. Even pros drill them constantly

Train smart, not hard. Technique first, intensity second.
Thinking of training in Thailand? Then check out our Train and stay options here

Next Steps

After two weeks of consistent training, revisit your form. Film yourself or ask an experienced trainer to critique your technique. Small adjustments compound over time.

Consider finding a boxing gym or coach. Even 2-3 sessions can accelerate your learning curve and prevent injuries that might sideline you.

And if you haven't already, watch that video on proper kicking technique again. One common mistake fixed is the difference between building strength and building injury.

Ready to start? Grab your hand wraps, get to the bag, and focus on form. Your future self will be grateful you didn't rush.

Have questions about heavy bag training? Feel free to contact us here

No. You do not have to fight

Do You Have to Fight if You Train at a Muay Thai Camp?

No. You do not have to fight. The majority of people who train at a Muay Thai camp never step into a competitive fight and that is completely fine. Muay Thai training is for everyone, fighters and non-fighters alike.

Why do people think fighting is required?

Because Muay Thai has deep roots in competitive fighting, people assume that joining a camp means signing up for a bout. This is a common misconception. Training and competing are two completely separate things.

What do most people actually do at a Muay Thai camp?

Most people come to get fit, learn a new skill, experience authentic Thai culture, or challenge themselves physically and mentally. They train hard, learn technique, and leave in better shape than when they arrived. No fight required.

Who does choose to fight?

Some people, usually those who have been training for a while and want to test themselves, choose to take on a competitive bout. This is always a personal decision and never something that is pushed on anyone.

Is Muay Thai safe for beginners?

Yes. Good camps structure their classes so beginners train at their own level. Pad work, bag work, and technique drills are the foundation of every session, in fact at Phuket King we ar one of the few Gyms that has a Technique of the day, every day. Sparring sounds scary, the thought of you getting pitched against a Muay Thai Warrior, in reality, soaring is great fun, and should be tried as soon as you have the skills and feel comfortable. The gym will make sure everyone knows that it's fun, light and relaxed. Of course, its always optional and you are ultimately in charge of your experience.,
Check our package builder here for an idea of costs

What should a beginner expect at a Muay Thai camp?

Expect to learn the basics, strikes, kicks, footwork, and movement, in a supportive environment. Coaches will work with your level and push you at a pace that is right for you. Most beginners surprise themselves within the first few sessions.

Can anyone train at a Muay Thai camp?

Yes. Men, women, all ages, all fitness levels. You do not need any martial arts background. You just need to show up.

You can take a look at our prices here, but remember, message us anytime. We're more than happy to help.

Am I Too Old to Learn Muay Thai? | Phuket King Muay Thai

One of our students is 67 years old. They train at Phuket King Muay Thai, go back to Europe, and then come back again. They keep coming back because it helps their mobility and because they love it. In fact one of the main reasons they come to Thailand in the first place is for the warmth, an dhow it helps his body. He has been coming to PKMT for about 3 years now, and every November, turns up ready to learn.

That is the answer to your question.

But let me give you a bit more than that.

Age changes how you train. It does not stop you.

You Recover slower when you are older. That is real and worth knowing before you arrive. You will not bounce back from two sessions a day the same way a 22 year old does. A good trainer knows this and adjusts accordingly. At PKMT we structure training around the individual in front of us, not a fixed programme that ignores where you actually are physically.

Flexibility and mobility are key also. This is actually one of the reasons older students respond so well to Muay Thai. The warm up, the movement drills, the hip rotation not to mention the herbal sauna, all help with mobility and ecovery. They become part of your daily rhythm and your body starts to respond in ways that surprise most people.

What older students have that younger ones often do not

Patience. Focus. A genuine reason for being there.

Older students are not here to impress anyone. They are not distracted. They listen to their trainer, they apply the correction, and they improve. Some of the most technically clean students we have trained came to Muay Thai later in life precisely because they had the discipline to absorb it properly.

What to tell your trainer before you start

Be honest about any injuries or conditions before your first session. A knee issue changes how you drill kicks. A shoulder problem changes your pad combinations. This is not a problem, it is just useful information that helps your trainer build sessions that work for your body rather than against it.

The mobility question

This comes up more with older students than any other benefit, and it makes sense. Muay Thai requires your whole body to move. Your hips, your shoulders, your ankles, your core. Training consistently loosens everything up. Students who arrive stiff leave moving better. Students who come back regularly keep that mobility in a way that most other exercise does not deliver.

Our 67-year-old student figured that out. That is why they keep coming back.

The truth about age and Muay Thai

The people who worry most about being too old are usually the ones who get the most out of it. They arrive without ego, they work hard, they listen, and they leave with something real.

If you are thinking about trying Muay Thai but worried you are too old, that you missed the boat, maybe you have a little niggle: don't. You will be fine. Just learn to manage yourself and tell the coaches about any injuries.

Age is not your obstacle. Not starting is.

Book your training at phuketking.com

Frequently Asked Questions

Am I too old to learn Muay Thai?

No. Students in their 40s, 50s, and beyond train regularly at Phuket King Muay Thai. One of our students is 67 and continues to return from Europe to train because of the mobility and fitness benefits.

Is Muay Thai hard on your body as you get older?

Less than most people expect. Muay Thai is a fluid discipline. You are always rotating and relaxed on impact, which makes it softer on your joints than activities like running or football. Recovery time does increase with age, which is why training is structured around the individual.

What are the benefits of Muay Thai for older adults?

Improved mobility, functional strength, cardiovascular fitness, and mental focus are the most commonly reported benefits. Many older students find the mobility improvements alone are worth the training.

What if I have an existing injury?

Tell your trainer before your first session. A good coach will build your sessions around your injury, not through it. This applies to any age but matters more the older you are.

How to Book a Muay Thai Camp in Phuket (And Actually Show Up Ready)

Now comes the part most people overthink: actually booking it. This guide cuts through the noise and walks you through exactly how to book a Muay Thai camp in Phuket, what to look for, and how to make sure your first session does not wreck you.

Step 1: Decide What You Actually Want From This

Before you book anything, get clear on one thing: what does a good trip look like for you?

There are three types of people who come to Phuket to train:

The fitness traveller. You want to train hard, sweat more than you ever have at home, lose some weight, and come back with a story. You have never done Muay Thai before or you have done a few classes. You want guidance, not a fight contract.

The serious hobbyist. You train back home. You want two sessions a day with real Thai trainers who will actually push your technique, not just let you hit pads for an hour.

The fighter. You have bouts coming up. You need specific preparation, sparring, and a trainer who knows what they are doing at competition level.

Phuket has gyms for all three. Know which one you are before you book. It changes everything from the training intensity to the accommodation, the schedule, and how long you should stay.

Phuket is not small. Where your gym sits matters.

Kathu sits in the centre of the island. Quieter than Patong, closer than the southern tips, easy access to everything without the chaos of the tourist strip. It is where you come when you want to actually train, not just take Instagram photos of a ring.

Phuket King Muay Thai is based in Kathu, right on the lake. The setting matters: when you are training twice a day and your body is asking questions, having space to breathe, recover, and reset makes a real difference.

Qualified trainers with fight experience. Ask who the trainers are. At PKMT, Kru Max, Kru Frong, and Kru Pot have all competed at serious levels. You want people who have been in the ring, not just held pads.

Small class sizes. Big camps can run 30 or 40 students per session. That means less time on pads with a trainer and more time waiting. Smaller camps give you actual attention.

Accommodation on site or nearby. Commuting to training twice a day is exhausting. Staying at or near the gym keeps your recovery time protected and your schedule clean.

Get some cardio in your legs. Even 20 minutes of running a few times a week before you fly helps. Training twice a day is hard on your cardiovascular system early on.

Bring the right gear. While most gyms do lend out gloves, hand wraps and shinguards, it is worth brining your own if you have them already, or purchasing some on your arrival. Borrowing is a short term fix, but having your own is just better, more hygienic, and well, it's yours.

How to Choose the Right Muay Thai Gym for You (And Stop Getting Blinded by Belts)

Let me be direct: every good Muay Thai gym in Thailand will have pictures of ex-fighters on the wall.

Most of them will have a trainer with a Lumpinee belt. Many will have multiple trainers who fought at Ratchadamnoen. Some will have won provincial titles. All of this looks impressive on Instagram. All of this is also useless for deciding if that gym is actually good for you.

Here is why.

The Belt Trap

In Thailand, the career path for most fighters is straightforward. You start young, fight for 10 to 15 years, win some belts along the way because the sheer volume of fights means you are bound to win something somewhere, and then you retire. What comes next? You either become a pad holder, open a gym, or try to train fighters. That is the system.

This means there are hundreds, maybe thousands, of ex-fighters and ex-champions in Thailand right now running gyms and holding pads. A belt means that person could fight. It does not mean they can teach you. It does not mean they care about your progress. And it definitely does not mean the gym is well run.

Think about it differently. Look at professional football. The best managers in the world are not necessarily the best footballers who ever played. In fact, many of them never even made it as professional players. What made them great managers was something completely different: the ability to see talent, teach technique, organise systems, and care about getting the best out of people.

Same logic applies to Muay Thai. A championship belt says one thing: that person was a good fighter. It says nothing about whether they are a good coach, whether they give a damn about you, or whether the gym is worth your money and time.

What Actually Matters: The Real Checklist

When you are evaluating a gym, forget the belts for a minute. Look for these things instead.

Is the gym well structured?

Walk in and observe. Are there regular technique classes with progression? Or is it just open mat time where everyone does their own thing? Does the schedule make sense? Can you follow a learning path, or are you left to figure it out yourself?

A well-run gym has a system. Beginners learn fundamentals in a separate class. There is pad work progression. There are conditioning sessions. Sparring happens at appropriate times with appropriate partners. This is not sexy. It will not make it onto a promotional video. But it is what actually teaches you Muay Thai.

Do the coaches actually coach?

There is a massive difference between a pad holder and a coach.

A pad holder holds the pads, you punch and kick, session ends. A coach watches your stance, stops you mid-combination to correct your hip rotation, tells you why your timing is off, and adjusts the drill to challenge you at exactly the right level. A coach cares whether you get better.

Watch a class before you commit. Do the trainers give feedback, or do they stand there checking their phone? Are they correcting technique, or just letting you hit hard? Are they pushing you to improve, or just collecting your money?

What is the culture of the gym?

This matters more than people think. Walk around. How do the experienced students treat beginners? Are they welcoming, or are they cliquey? Do people actually help each other, or is it competitive in a bad way?

In Thailand especially, you will often find that you are welcomed warmly when you arrive, money changes hands, and then you become invisible. You get pushed to the side. You are no longer special. This is so common it should be your baseline expectation unless the gym proves otherwise.

A good gym feels different. People know your name after a week. Trainers remember what you worked on last session. Senior students will help you with your wraps or give you feedback on your technique. The energy is about collective progress, not just selling packages.

Does the gym philosophy match what you actually want?

Every gym has a vibe. Some are all about fighting and competition. Some are fitness-focused. Some genuinely want to teach you the art. Some just want to move volume through their doors.

Be honest about what you want. If you want to compete, choose a gym where most people are training toward that goal. If you want fitness and technique, do not go to a hardcore fight camp expecting a relaxed learning environment. If you want to travel and train without pressure, avoid camps that are purely about producing fighters.

About Us

The Feeling Test

Here is the simplest test: how do you feel when you walk out after your first session?

Tired? Good. That is normal.

Excited to come back? Better. That means the session was structured well and you got something out of it.

Ignored? Red flag. The gym took your money and did not think about your experience beyond that.

Confused about what to work on next? Red flag. A good gym tells you your next focus.

Rushed through drills without correction? Red flag. Volume over quality is a business model, not a training approach.

The Questions to Ask Before You Commit

When you contact a gym, ask these directly. Their answers will tell you everything.

What is your beginner progression like? If they answer with something vague or push you toward private sessions immediately, that is not a good sign. A real gym will explain the structure clearly.

How do you assess your students? Do they watch you? Do they understand your level? Or do they just throw you in with everyone else?

What happens after the first week? This is the one that separates good gyms from average ones. Week one is always exciting. What about week three when you are sore and questioning everything? Does the gym adjust your training, check in on your goals, and help you stay committed?

Can I watch a class before I book? Any gym worth training at will let you sit and watch. If they push back on this, that is a signal.

Why This Matters at Phuket King Muay Thai

We have trainers with real fight experience. Kru Max and Kru Ris, Kru Pot have immense ring experience. But that is not why people train here and come back year after year.

They come back because the gym is structured. Because there are beginner classes, intermediate technique sessions, and advanced pad work. Because the trainers remember what you worked on and adjust accordingly. Because someone asks you on day four how your body is holding up and whether you want to dial back the intensity or push harder. We put an emphasis on Coaching standards. How to identify what you the student needs ch have all been in the ring at serious levels.

They come back because the environment is built on actually giving a damn. Not just about collecting money, but about whether you leave Thailand a better martial artist than when you arrived.

That philosophy runs through everything: the class structure, the accommodation on site, the cafe, the ice bath, the herbal sauna. Every part of it is designed so that training is sustainable and you can focus on getting better instead of managing logistics.

The Bottom Line

Stop looking at belts. Start looking at systems, coaches, and culture.

The best gym for you is not the one with the most impressive credentials on the wall. It is the one where you feel like you are being taught, where the trainers care about your progress, where the structure makes sense, and where you actually want to come back.

Go watch a class. Talk to current students. Ask hard questions. Trust your gut on the feeling you get when you walk in the door.

That instinct will tell you everything you need to know.
